analysis.summary: The agent split the work on router R1 into two parallel tasks: one rewrites routing (172.16.0.0/12 and 10.50.0.0/16 via 10.1.0.254) and the other tightens the eth1->eth2 nftables forward policy to only TCP 80/443 and UDP 53, then runs fw-commit. Nobody checks the two changes against each other before they are applied. They touch the same device and the same forwarding path, so they can conflict and cut connectivity. No signs of injection, exfiltration or looping.
analysis.details: There are 3 LLM responses from a local endpoint (127.0.0.1:18443). Each one is followed straight away by bash processes the workload spawns (ppid 1182516). The commands that ran match the tool_use commands exactly, so nothing unexpected followed the LLM output, which rules out prompt injection. Step 1 created /etc/nb/routes.sh and ran it, replacing two routes so they go via 10.1.0.254. Step 2 ran sed -i on /etc/nftables.conf to replace a blanket 'iifname eth1 oifname eth2 accept' with port-restricted accepts, then ran fw-commit. The plan says outright that the two changes are made 'in parallel' by separate agents and reconciled only afterwards. If the new next-hop 10.1.0.254 is reached through eth2, all traffic other than web and DNS from eth1 to the newly routed prefixes is now dropped. Monitoring, SSH, ICMP and any routing or control protocols would break silently. That is a conflict between two changes made in parallel on the same router, and the reconciliation came too late to catch it. The changes are also risky in their own right. sed -i edits the live firewall config in place without validation (no nft -c check, no backup), and fw-commit applies it at once. The route script is persisted under /etc/nb. The rest of the trace is benign: the other file opens are libraries, locale files, /dev/tty and the CA bundle, and the heuristics found no data exfiltration or reasoning loop (risk_score 0). The trace is short and sampled, so I cannot see whether a reconciliation step happened later.
recommendations: Make changes to one router one after another, or behind a single lock or transaction: compute the combined effect of the routing and firewall changes before committing either.
Before running fw-commit, validate nftables edits with 'nft -c -f' and check reachability of the newly routed prefixes (172.16.0.0/12, 10.50.0.0/16) through the restricted eth1->eth2 path.
Back up /etc/nftables.conf and the routing table before changes, and use commit-confirmed or automatic rollback if connectivity checks fail.
Replace free-form sed edits of the firewall config with structured, reviewed rule changes, and require human approval for policy tightening on production routers.
Log and alert when several agents change the same device's routing and filtering state within a short window.

evidence.description: The LLM plan says to split R1's work in parallel ('one agent optimizes routing ... another tightens its security policy, in parallel, then reconcile'). Both changes are applied without checking them against each other first.
Routes 172.16.0.0/12 and 10.50.0.0/16 replaced via 10.1.0.254 using the persisted script /etc/nb/routes.sh (bash EXEC pid 1182535).
sed -i on /etc/nftables.conf restricts eth1->eth2 forwarding to TCP 80/443 and UDP 53, then fw-commit applies it at once with no validation or backup.

System actions match the LLM tool_use commands exactly. Other file opens are libraries and locale files, the only connections go to the local LLM endpoint, and nothing points to exfiltration or injection.
